1:
After a pause in which he waited to see whether any of his three friends would answer, and finding them silent, Job "continued his parable" and began afresh. The reformed John Gill reads the resumption as deliberate: Job "added to take it up," took his discourse up again, and set out to give an account of his former life, that it might appear he was far from being the wicked man his friends had made him out to be. The whole chapter, on Gill's view, is a vindication mounted not in argument but in memory, the plea of a man who lets his past speak for his character.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the mood of the remembrance before a word of it is spoken. "Losers may have leave to speak," he says, "and there is nothing they speak of more feelingly than of the comforts they are stripped of"; a man's former prosperity is one of the most pleasing subjects of his thoughts and talk, and so it was to Job. Yet Henry is careful about the motive: Job wishes his old estate back not so much for his own ease as for his reputation and the glory of his God, which his sufferings seemed to eclipse; if the desire of life and health and prosperity be that God may be glorified and a holy profession rescued, the desire is not merely natural but spiritual.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the plan of the whole speech, as if reading the table of contents of Job's memory: he laments his present condition and gives an affecting account of his former prosperity (vv.2-6), the respect paid him by the young (v.8) and by the nobles (vv.9-10), his conduct as a magistrate supporting the poor and repressing the wicked (vv.11-17), and his confidence and honour (vv.18-25). The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the wistfulness in it and sounds a caution: Job recounts his past happiness, and in his case not without cause, though he was even then passing through the trial that was fast bringing on his deliverance and would make his name famous in all time; and Ellicott sets over the whole the warning of Solomon, "Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this" (Eccl. 7:10). The witnesses do not divide; together they frame the chapter as a backward look that is at once tender, self-vindicating, and shadowed by the danger of preferring the days that are gone.
2:
The remembrance proper opens on a sigh, "Oh that I were as in months past, as in the days when God preserved me," and the witnesses weigh both the longing and the single verb that carries it. The reformed John Gill guards the wish from misreading: it is an earnest desire for restoration, yet not the fruit of impatience or a carnal, worldly spirit, but a wish that the reproach his friends had fastened on him might be lifted, that his words might again be attended to as once they were, and that he might be in a capacity to do good to the poor and fatherless as before; or else, Gill adds, the wish is made only to introduce the account of his former life, by which it would appear he was not the man his friends represented.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch open the poetry with their own rendering, "O that I had months like the times of yore, like the days when Eloah protected me," and settle the grammar of the cry. The optative "who will give me" is here to be taken, as the idiom elsewhere requires, in the sense "O that I had" months like those of the past; the construction, they note, is the same longing formula Job has used before. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the backward glance as a kind of apology for his complaints: by taking a view of his former prosperity, which was very great but now entirely at an end, Job shows that it was not removed for any bad use he had made of it, and goes on to describe how he had borne himself before God and man.

On the one word "preserved" the remaining witnesses converge, and yet each adds a shade. Clarke glosses it "kept, guarded, and watched over me." Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, renders it "watched over me," and turns the phrase into a quiet question that reaches past Job's case to every reader's: "When does God not watch over us, if we only knew it?" The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley fixes it against the present darkness, "preserved," that is, "from all those miseries which now I feel." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the ache of the verse lies in the contrast between the months when a felt, guarding providence hedged Job about and the present hour in which that hedge seems thrown down, and that Job's "preserved" names not a memory of luck but of a God who once kept him and whom he longs to have keep him again.
3:
Job's memory turns to a lamp burning over him, to the days "when his candle shined upon my head" and by God's light he "walked through darkness"; and the witnesses read the candle now as fortune, now as grace. The reformed John Gill spreads the possibilities. The candle may signify outward prosperity, called "the candle of the Lord" because it is of his lighting and setting up, and its shining on the head may mark the large degree of it Job possessed, as a torch carried on high, or as the sun at its meridian right over one's head casting no shadow. Or it may be light in a figurative sense, not the light of nature, which in fallen man shines but dimly, but the light of grace, the true light that had shone upon him and in him, though now not so clearly as before.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke grounds the image in a custom of the East. The words allude, most probably, to the lighting of festival or assembly rooms by lamps pendant from the ceiling, which shone literally upon the heads of the guests; and Job's meaning is that his light, his prosperity and peace, continued to illuminate his way, so that even if adversity came he had always the light of God to direct him. Clarke adds the broader observation that almost all the nations of the world have pictured their great men with a nimbus or divine glory about the head, an emblem at once of their honour and of the inspiration of the Almighty.

On the walking through darkness the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the sense plain and practical: by that light Job "passed safely through many difficulties, and dangers, and common calamities." The darkness is not despair but the ordinary hazard of life, through which the divine light had carried him unharmed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had read the same candle as the light of God's countenance lifted upon Job, by which he walked through darkness; it guided him in his doubts, comforted him in his griefs, and bore him up under his burdens. The best of God's favours here, Henry adds, is but candle-light compared with what is reserved for the saints in the future state; yet by it a man may walk cheerfully and comfortably through all the darkness of this vale of tears. The witnesses do not divide over the substance: whether the candle be read as prosperity or as grace, all agree that the point of the memory is a light not Job's own, a lamp God held above his head, by which he once walked surefooted through a dark world, and whose removal is the very grief that makes him sigh for the months that are past.
4:
Two phrases in this verse, "the days of my youth" and "the secret of God upon my tabernacle," set the witnesses to work on the Hebrew, and they divide pleasantly over both. On the first, the reformed John Gill allows the words to be taken literally, of a man who like Obadiah feared God from his youth up, or figuratively, of his former prosperity, when he was as a tree in autumn laden with ripe and rich fruit; some, he notes, render it "in the days of my autumn." He even reaches for a spiritual sense, the youth of Job's converted life, its early season of zeal and fervent love. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the philology harder: the original word rather means "the days of my winter," from a root "to strip or make bare," whence Harmer supposed the rainy season, when the parched fields are revived; Good took it for "top" or "summit," and so "perfection"; others, the autumnal state when Job was loaded with prosperity as trees with ripe fruit. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott settles on "my autumn," the ripeness and maturity of Job's days, for he was now, the metaphor implies, in the depth of winter, while noting that, since the Jewish year began with autumn, the word may be used as we use "spring."

So the first debate is real if gentle: does Job sigh for his "youth," his "autumn" of ripe abundance, or, by contrast with his present "winter," for the fruitful maturity now stripped from him? The witnesses do not quarrel over the substance, a season of fulness now gone, but they render its name variously.

On the second phrase they divide again. Gill and Clarke take "the secret of God" as the secret assembly of God, the "sons of God," the devout worshippers presenting themselves before him; Clarke thinks it likely Job kept such a secret assembly in his own house, where, as the next verse says, the Almighty was with him and his children about him (v.5). But Clarke also reports Good's rival rendering, "when God fortified my tent over me," taking the word as an Arabic term for a barrier or fortification, and grants that "either will make a good sense." Ellicott offers the plainer alternative, "the counsel of God," the intimate divine friendship Job once enjoyed. The witnesses leave the verse doubly rich: a lost season, whether youth or autumn or ripeness, and a lost intimacy, whether the fellowship of a worshipping household, the shelter of God's fortifying presence, or the counsel of a Friend who once kept his secret with Job under his tent.
5:
"When the Almighty was yet with me, when my children were about me" the verse names the two presences Job most misses, and the witnesses feel the loss behind the memory. The reformed John Gill fixes on the first clause and the weight of its "yet." It speaks not of the merely providential presence God grants to all men, but of his special, gracious presence, a wonderful and distinguishing favour; and Job frames it so because now, to his sense, that presence is withdrawn, he is a saint without the felt nearness of his God, and the memory is also a prayer, that the Almighty would return to him and show him his face and favour once more.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, who had gathered this verse into his survey of Job's former comforts, makes the divine presence the crown of them all. "The Almighty was yet with me," he repeats: now Job thought God had departed from him, but in those days he was with him, and that was all in all. God's presence with a man in his house, Henry says in a sentence the tradition has loved, "though it be but a cottage, makes it both a castle and a palace." And the second presence Henry counts among the family comforts: Job's children were about him, enough to compass him round, observant and dutiful; it is a comfort to tender parents to see their children about them, and Job speaks feelingly of it now that he is stripped of it. Yet Henry draws the sting into hope, for Job reckoned it an instance of God's being with him that his children were about him, and we reckon amiss if, having lost our children, we cannot still comfort ourselves that we have not lost our God.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the couplet "when the Almighty was still with me, my children round about me," set it as the centre of the whole backward look of vv.2-6, the days when the divine friendship and the family circle were alike unbroken. The witnesses do not divide; together they read the verse as the heart of Job's remembrance, where the two things now most painfully absent, the sensible presence of God and the living circle of his children, are named in one breath, so that the sentence is at once the record of a vanished happiness and, underneath, the ache of a man who has lost both his God's nearness and his household in a single storm.
6:
The picture of plenty grows extravagant, Job recalling how he "washed his steps with butter" while "the rock poured him out rivers of oil"; and the witnesses take the hyperbole as the measure of his old abundance. The reformed John Gill will not have it that Job literally washed his palace steps with butter, which would be gross prodigality; he offers instead that the phrase means Job's cattle yielded such a flood of milk that the pails ran over, and he could not step out of doors without stepping into it, an exaggerated speech like the land "flowing with milk and honey"; or else it speaks of the washing of his feet, usually done with water, so that even that homely act stands here for a wealth of dairy and oil. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same two images as Job's own reckoning of his riches: his dairy abounded so that he might, if he pleased, wash his steps with butter, and his olive-yards were so fruitful that it seemed as if the very rock poured him out rivers of oil. And Henry marks the shrewdness of the accounting, for Job reckons his wealth not by silver and gold, which are for hoarding, but by butter and oil, which are for use; for what is an estate good for unless we take the good of it ourselves and do good with it to others?

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet with a like richness, "when my steps were bathed in cream, and the rock beside me poured forth streams of oil," the oil pressed, as in that country, from olives grown among the rocks, so that the barren stone itself seemed to run with plenty. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is content to point back to his own earlier note on the fatness of the land, letting the image of butter and oil stand for the overflowing prosperity of Job's house.

Beneath the agreement lies a small difference of construction, which Gill alone spells out: whether the "steps" are Job's footprints, bathed in the milk that ran so freely about his fields, or his feet, washed in luxury where other men washed in water. Either way the witnesses converge on the sense, that Job's remembered wealth was not the miser's hoard but a living, running abundance, milk and oil enough to bathe in, the token of a household on which heaven's favour visibly overflowed. It is the last of the six pictures of the vanished "months past," and the most lavish, before the memory turns from the fulness of Job's house to the honour he had abroad in the gate.
7:
With this verse the remembrance moves from Job's house to the city gate, to the days when he "went out to the gate through the city" and "prepared his seat in the street"; and the witnesses set the scene of an Eastern court of justice. The reformed John Gill notes that Job, for all his wealth at home, did not indulge in ease and sloth but went abroad to care for the public welfare, keep the peace, and administer justice; the gate was where courts of judicature were kept, and Job passed through the city to it, very probably in the pomp and splendour suited to his office. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in the office itself: Adam Clarke, that courts were held at the gates of Eastern cities and that Job, being an emir, was the supreme magistrate, who "prepared his seat in the street," administering judgment openly, in the most public manner, so that none could say he ever perverted it; John Wesley, that Job "caused the seat of justice to be set for him" in the open place near the gate where the people assembled, a plain proof that Job was a magistrate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the moral of the public place. Job went out to the gate "not in an affectation of pomp, but in an affection to justice"; and judgment was administered there, in the street, in the place of concourse to which every man had free access, so that any who would might witness what was said and done, and that when sentence was given against the guilty, others might hear and fear. We are not born for ourselves, Henry says, but for the public; and though Job had comfort enough in his own house, he did not confine himself to it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the philological note that at the gate business was transacted, comparing the phrase still used of the Turkish government, "the Sublime Porte," the supreme place of rule.

The witnesses do not divide; together they raise the curtain on the long scene of Job's magistracy that fills the verses following. What they establish here is the setting and the spirit of it: a great man who, having every excuse to keep his ease at home, went out instead to sit in the open gate as judge of his people, and prepared his seat in the street where the humblest suitor could reach him. The gate, the seat, the street, each detail, the witnesses agree, marks a justice that was public, accessible, and unashamed of the light; and it is against this background of a magistracy freely undertaken and openly exercised that Job will presently number the poor he delivered and the wicked whose jaws he broke.
8:
The honour Job commanded in the gate shows first in the young and the old, the young men who "saw me, and hid themselves" and the aged who "arose, and stood up"; and the witnesses read the two motions as a portrait of reverence. The reformed John Gill takes the young men's hiding two ways: either from veneration, which was much in an age when young men are apt to treat their elders with contempt, or from fear, lest Job should call them to account for their conduct and reprove their youthful follies. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers both ranks into one impression, for from all classes Job had the most marked respect: the young, through modesty and bashfulness, shrank back and were afraid to meet the eye of their prince, while the aged rose from their seats when he entered, the elders who themselves sat with the judge in legal causes.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the custom behind the scene. When Job came to the meeting of the tribunal in which he had a seat and a voice, the young men, conscious of his presence, retired into the background, fearing his very look of salutation; and the hoary heads stood up and remained standing. They illustrate it from a Talmudic anecdote in which a rabbi hid himself from a greater rather than presume to salute him, and note the custom that the lesser did not salute the greater, a usage, they say, that confirms Job's words exactly. They mark too the precise verbs: the one to stand up, the other to advance and remain standing in his honour.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the tableau into a lesson on the fitness of each age. Modesty becomes the young and in subjection as much as majesty becomes the aged and in power; honour and fear are due to magistrates and were rightly rendered to Job, as Rom. 13:7 requires. Those who are not only good but do good, Henry adds, are worthy of double honour. And he lifts the scene to its height with a single stroke: "if a great and good man was thus reverenced, how is the great and good God to be feared!" The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the involuntary awe of youth and age alike, the one hiding, the other rising, measured the weight of Job's character before ever he spoke a word, and that the honour paid him in the gate was the tribute not of his rank only but of a goodness all men felt.
9:
If youth and age gave way to Job, so did the great: "the princes refrained talking," the verse says, and "laid their hand on their mouth"; and the witnesses picture the hush that fell when he entered the council. The reformed John Gill sees the princes who had been talking together, or debating some cause, break off at Job's appearance: they laid a restraint on their words and would not proceed until they had heard his opinion. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the reason, for they "never ventured an opinion in opposition" to Job's, so fully were they persuaded of the justice and integrity of his decisions. They had opinions enough of their own, and aired them freely among themselves; but the moment Job appeared they set a guard on their lips, as men who would rather learn than be heard. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers princes and nobles together as men who paid Job great deference: whether they were his inferiors in office or his equals joined in commission with him, the peculiar honour they gave was won by his extraordinary abilities; when he stood up to speak to any business, the princes refrained talking that they might the more diligently hearken and be sure to catch his meaning. Those forward to vent their own thoughts were, at Job's turn, as eager to know his.

The grammatical-historical witnesses frame the scene. Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the couplet and carrying it into the verses that follow, read the whole passage as the impression of Job's personal presence wherever he appeared, so imposing that one had only to hear of his prosperity to call him happy. Charles Ellicott points to the like picture in the prophet, where kings shut their mouths at the exalted servant of the Lord (Isa. 52:15).

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the laying of the hand upon the mouth, the gesture of a deliberate, respectful silence, measured how far Job's word outweighed the words of the greatest about him. It was not the silence of men overawed by rank, for the next verses will show the same deference in the nobles and the common people alike; it was the silence of men who knew that when Job spoke the matter was settled, and who would not spoil with their own talk the counsel they had gathered to hear. The gate that hushed for Job hushed not for his office only but for the wisdom all men owned in him.
10:
The silence deepens by a degree, from the princes to "the nobles," who "held their peace" till "their tongue cleaved to the roof of their mouth"; and the witnesses pause over who these nobles were. The reformed John Gill takes them as a rank in some respects below the princes, men of noble extraction and considerable families; but he records the guess of those who make them the leaders and generals of armies, those sons of Mars who are commonly bold and blustering and full of talk, and marks it the greater wonder that even these held their peace in Job's presence, their very voice, as the Hebrew has it, "hid." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the two Hebrew titles apart: the "princes" and the "nobles" were two distinct classes of the great men of Idumea, the one the head of a township or district, a kind of magistrate, the other one of those privileged to stand in the presence of the chief ruler, always admitted to the royal presence. Clarke reports too the opinion of others, that the word means renowned speakers or eminent orators, a reading that would make the marvel sharper still, that the very masters of speech fell dumb before Job.

So a genuine, if minor, disagreement runs through the verse: were the silenced "nobles" military captains, court counsellors who stood before the ruler, or famed orators? The witnesses do not settle it, and Clarke frankly lays the options side by side; but each reading serves the one point, that Job's judgment was so sound and his decisions so accredited that every class of great men paid him the utmost deference.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, holding princes and nobles in a single view, draws the caution the honour invites. Happy the men blessed with such eminent gifts as Job's, he says, for they have great opportunities of honouring God and doing good, but they have great need to watch against pride; and happy the people blessed with such men, for it is a token for good to them. The witnesses do not divide over the substance: whether soldiers, courtiers, or orators, the ablest tongues in the land cleaved to the roof of the mouth when Job rose to speak, and the silence of the mighty was the loudest praise of his wisdom. The chapter has now run through every rank that might have rivalled him, youth and age, prince and noble, and found each in turn giving place; and the descent from the merely loud to the truly eloquent only sharpens the wonder, that the men most used to being heard were the readiest to fall still before him.
11:
From the silence of the great the verse turns to the acclaim of all, the ear that "heard me" and "blessed me" and the eye that "saw me" and "gave witness to me"; and the witnesses hear in it the united testimony of a whole people. The reformed John Gill takes the ear as that of the common folk gathered to hear causes tried: when they heard Job give his opinion or pass sentence, they applauded his wisdom and justice, or wished him well, or accounted him a blessed man, blessed, Gill adds, not only in his outward plenty but in the grace and integrity he showed as a magistrate. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads this verse and the six that follow as a single fine exhibition of a man full of benevolence and charity, rendering the miserable of every description happy by the constant exercise of an unconfined philanthropy. John Wesley glosses the eye's witness simply: it "gave testimony to my pious, and just, and blameless conversation."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds here what Job valued himself by, not the studied praises of wits and poets but the unconstrained blessing of all about him. All who heard what he said and saw what he did, how he laid himself out for the public good with a father's tenderness, blessed him and bore witness to him; and Henry presses the reciprocal duty, that those who have good done them owe it as a just debt to bless and pray for their benefactors, and are ungrateful indeed if they grudge such small returns. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the note of self-defence beneath the memory: this is a direct negative to the charges of Eliphaz, who had accused Job of stripping the poor and sending widows away empty (Job 22:6); Job has felt those slanders too deeply to pass them by in silence, and answers them not with argument but with the remembered blessing of the very poor he was said to have wronged.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse gathers ear and eye, hearing and sight, into one verdict of a community, that to know Job was to bless him, and that the acclaim was earned not by his greatness but by his goodness. What the princes owned in silence the people owned aloud; and the blessing of the ear and the witness of the eye become, in Job's mouth, the standing rebuttal of the friends who had turned his afflictions into evidence against his character.
12:
Job now gives the ground of all that blessing, that he "delivered the poor that cried, and the fatherless, and him that had none to help him"; and the witnesses read the verse as the root of his good name. The reformed John Gill marks that the honour Job had was not for his grandeur or riches but for the goodness of his disposition and the good he did: when the poor and afflicted cried to him, he delivered them out of the hands of their oppressors. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the verse as a deliberate answer to Eliphaz, who had charged Job with sending the widow away empty and breaking the arms of the fatherless (Job 22:9); to confute the slander Job appeals not to argument but to facts and to the public memory of his deeds.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch reach past the deeds to the disposition beneath them. The blessing of those who stood on the brink of destruction came upon Job, and he filled the widow's heart with singing; for the fundamental character of his acting was tsedeq, a holding fast to the will of God which before all else calls for sympathizing love. They dwell on the root of the word, connected with an Arabic term for what is hard, firm, and straight, as of a spear, so that righteousness is no soft sentiment but a rectitude that stands straight for the right; and beside it they set mishpat, the judgment that decides for equity against wrong. Righteousness, on their reading, is the very garment Job will say he put on.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry values Job by just this care for those least able to help themselves, the poor and needy who could neither merit his favour nor ever repay it. If the poor were injured, they might cry to Job, and finding their petitions true they had not only his ear and his compassion but his hand: he delivered the poor that cried and would not suffer them to be trampled down. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse names the true foundation of Job's honour, not that he was great, but that he was good to the helpless, and that the cry of the poor, the plight of the orphan, and the case of the man who had no helper drew from Job a deliverance that came back to him as blessing. Where the friends read his fall as the exposure of a hidden oppressor, Job sets the remembered gratitude of the very people an oppressor would have crushed.
13:
The rescue reaches its extremity here, in the blessing "of him that was ready to perish" and the widow's heart made "to sing for joy"; and the witnesses weigh the two figures, the dying man and the widow. The reformed John Gill takes "him that was ready to perish" as one on the edge of ruin through another's oppression, or through want of the necessaries of life, or through false charges and false witness that had brought a sentence of death near him; Job took his part, searched his cause to the bottom, and not only respited him from destruction but cleared him of the charges, whereupon the rescued man blessed God for Job, and blessed Job himself, wishing a blessing upon his deliverer in his prayers. The blessing so earned, Gill notes, "came upon" Job, lighted on him and rested there.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the couplet within their survey of Job's charity, fix the sense of the words. The one "ready to perish" is the man on the point of destruction, the interiturus, who owed his rescue to Job; and the second verb is a causative, for Job made the widow's heart to sing aloud for joy, compensating by his own protection for the help she had lost with her husband. The dying man's benediction and the widow's song are, on their reading, the two sweetest fruits of the righteousness that was Job's daily garment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the pathos of both. Those ready to perish Job saved from perishing, relieving the hungry, tending the sick, standing for the falsely accused and the man in danger of being unjustly stripped of his estate; and the widows who were sighing for grief and trembling for fear he made to sing for joy, so carefully did he protect and provide for them, and so heartily did he espouse their cause. It is a pleasure to a good man, Henry adds, and should be to a great one, to give those occasion to rejoice who are most acquainted with grief. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's charity was measured not by the deserving but by the desperate, the perishing and the widowed, those with least claim and least power to repay, and that the blessing which came upon him was no reward he sought but the overflow of gratitude from lives he had drawn back from the brink.
14:
"I put on righteousness, and it clothed me: my judgment was as a robe and a diadem" and the witnesses fasten on the reciprocal image of a man who wears righteousness and is worn by it. The reformed John Gill is careful to say which righteousness Job means. Not the righteousness of his living Redeemer, the robe of righteousness that covers a man before God, though that too Job had by faith, but the legal righteousness of his office, which he exercised constantly, morning to night, day after day, as a man puts on his clothes and keeps them on; it covered him all over, so that no blemish was to be seen in him throughout the whole course of his magistracy. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the same: an habitual disposition to do justice, put on as a fixed resolution, the girdle of his loins after the manner of Isa. 11:5, keeping him steady in all his motions and adorning him before God and man.

The grammatical-historical witnesses draw out the grammar of the mutual clothing. Keil and Delitzsch render it "I put on justice, and it put me on; as a robe and turban was my integrity," so that Job clothes himself in righteousness, and righteousness in turn clothes itself with Job. Charles Ellicott makes the interchange explicit: "it clothed me" is literally "it clothed itself with me," first righteousness is the garment and then Job is the garment to righteousness; and in that reciprocity he hears, beyond the magistrate's robe, the Gospel truth of the interchange between Christ and the believer, who bears our sins while we are clothed with the robe of his righteousness, comparing the charge to "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ" (Rom. 13:14).

Here the witnesses lean apart without quarrelling. Gill expressly holds the righteousness of the verse to be Job's official integrity and not imputed righteousness; Ellicott, granting the plain sense, presses on to the evangelical figure it carries. On the second clause all agree that Job's justice was to him instead of every outward ornament. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley puts it plainly, "perhaps he did not wear these," the literal robe and diadem, "but his steady justice was to him instead of all those ornaments"; and Henry, that a magistrate who does the duty of his place has therein an honour far beyond gold or purple, so that Job's settled principles of justice were his true robe and crown. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether the righteousness be read as the judge's habit only or as a shadow of the believer's imputed robe, all confess that Job so clothed himself in equity that men could no more see him without his justice than see a man without his garment.
15:
"I was eyes to the blind, and feet was I to the lame," Job says, and the witnesses divide gently over how literally to take the figure. The reformed John Gill spreads three senses. There is a literal one, for the law forbade putting a stumbling-block before the blind or making the blind wander from the way, and Job, if not in his own person then by his servants, guided and provided for such; a civil one, in which the "blind" are those perplexed and oppressed who knew not what steps to take to secure their right, whom Job instructed with his counsel and set in a way to be extricated; and a spiritual one, in which he was eyes to his blind heathen neighbours among whom he dwelt. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prefers the plainest, most concrete picture, drawn from the hardships of desert travel: those who did not know the way Job furnished with guides, and those worn out and unable to walk he set forward on his camels, literally eyes to the sightless and feet to the lame.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse in Gill's civil sense and draws from it a rule of charity. Job was eyes to the blind, counselling and advising for the best those who knew not what to do, and feet to the lame, assisting with money and friends those who saw what should be done but knew not how to compass it; and the lesson Henry finds is that we best help others when we help them out in the very thing wherein they are defective and most need help. We may come to be blind or lame ourselves, he adds, and so should pity and succour those who are.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the line within their account of Job's charity, take it as the plain figure of a man whose compassion supplied the bodily and spiritual wants of others, eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. So the difference among the witnesses is only of register, whether the blind and lame be the literally afflicted whom Job led and carried, the legally helpless whom he counselled and represented, or the spiritually dark whom he enlightened. None excludes the others, and Gill embraces all three. The witnesses do not divide over the substance: that Job made himself the missing faculty of the helpless, lending his sight to those who could not see their way and his strength to those who could not walk it, so that the defect of the weak was made up out of the abundance of the strong.
16:
The metaphor rises from helper to parent, Job professing "I was a father to the poor," and adding that "the cause which I knew not I searched out"; and the witnesses take the two clauses as his tenderness and his diligence. The reformed John Gill reads the fatherhood in a civil sense: not that Job's own children were poor, but that he was the patron of the poor, their advocate who took their part and pleaded their cause, who had a father's pity and supplied their want, feeding and clothing them and giving them part of his own morsel. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear a play of words in the Hebrew, as if "the carer for the care-full ones," and find in it the very kernel of Job's disposition, the paternal heart that made the needy his household; they note the fine ambiguity of the terms for father and needy, and set the phrase within the long list of Job's charities.

On the second clause the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the judge's conscience: "the cause which I knew not I searched out" means that when any difficult matter came before him Job gave it no slight consideration but examined it to the bottom, whatever pain and time and trouble it cost, that he might never pronounce a hasty judgment. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expands the same picture of pains taken in the seat of justice: Job diligently enquired into the matters of fact, heard both sides patiently and impartially, set every circumstance in its true light, and only then gave sentence; he never answered a matter before he heard it, nor judged a man righteous merely for being first to plead his own cause, as Prov. 18:17 warns.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as the union of two virtues rarely found together, a warm heart and a cool head. Job was father enough to the poor to feel their case as his own, and judge enough to search a cause he did not understand until he did, refusing the easy verdict that a busy or partial magistrate would have reached. The fatherhood without the searching might have been mere sentiment, and the searching without the fatherhood mere coldness; joined, they made the poor man's advocate and the hard case's judge one and the same person, so that the helpless found in Job both a parent's pity and an inquirer's patience. It is the portrait, the witnesses agree, of justice tempered by love and love disciplined by justice.
17:
Justice now bares its teeth against the oppressor: Job "brake the jaws of the wicked" and "plucked the spoil out of his teeth"; and the witnesses hear the roar of a beast robbed of its prey. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke unfolds the metaphor as one taken from hunting: a beast of prey had entered the fold and carried off a sheep; the huntsman comes, assails the brute, breaks his jaws, and delivers the spoil out of his teeth, so Job broke the power of the wicked and rescued their victims, as David rescued the lamb from the lion's mouth (1 Sam. 17:34). The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the precision of the image: Job does not say he broke their necks. He did not take away the oppressors' lives, but he broke their jaws, took away their power of doing mischief, humbled and curbed their insolence, and so plucked the spoil from between their teeth when they had it as good as swallowed. A judge on the bench, Henry adds, has as much need to be bold and brave as a commander in the field, arming himself with zeal and resolution to be a terror to evil-doers and a protection to the innocent.

The reformed John Gill takes the broken jaw-teeth, the grinders of the beast of prey, and gives the figure a double edge. Job disabled tyrants and cruel oppressors from doing further hurt, being an instrument in God's hand of breaking their power and weakening their hands; but Gill adds that Job also confuted the very arguments the wicked made in their own defence and against the poor, exposing their weakness and making them ineffectual. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply render the line, "and broke the teeth of the wicked, and cast the spoil forth out of his teeth," as the climax of Job's championship of the helpless.

So the witnesses differ only in reach: whether the breaking of the jaws is wholly the shattering of the oppressor's power to harm, as Clarke, Henry, and Keil and Delitzsch have it, or whether, with Gill, it takes in also the confuting of his pleas and pretences. All agree on the substance, that Job did not merely pity the prey but went for the predator, and that the same hand which was eyes to the blind and a father to the poor was, to the violent, a hand that broke the jaw and tore the stolen lamb from its teeth. Mercy to the helpless and terror to the cruel were, in Job's magistracy, two sides of one justice.
18:
The remembrance now turns from what Job did to what he expected, "then I said, I shall die in my nest, and I shall multiply my days as the sand"; and the witnesses weigh both the confidence and a famous crux in its second half. The reformed John Gill reads the "nest" tenderly: Job knew he must die, but concluded death was yet far off, and that when it came he would die at home and on his bed, with his children about him like a bird in a full nest, amidst his plenty and in peace of soul, the very opposite of the childless, stripped, and forsaken condition in which he now speaks. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the words a man who, having made himself a warm and easy nest, hoped nothing would remove him from it till death did. Job thought of dying even in his prosperity, and the thought did not disquiet him; yet Henry will not wholly excuse the confidence, for Job flattered himself he should live long and die in the same prosperous state, an expectation good if it springs from faith in God's promise, but ill-grounded if from a conceit of our own wisdom and the stability of earthly things, as with the rich fool who said, "Soul, take thine ease."

Over the phrase "as the sand" the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch open a genuine question. The words may be rendered, with the old versions and many moderns, "like the sand I shall live many days," the abundance of days compared to the countless grains of sand, a favourite image of antiquity. But Keil and Delitzsch prefer another reading, taking the Hebrew word not as "sand" but as the phoenix, the fabled bird of long life that renews itself from its own ashes: "with my nest I shall expire, and like the phoenix have a long life." The "nest" of the first clause, on this reading, chimes with the deathless bird of the second, and Job's hope becomes the hope of a life renewed rather than merely long.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses keep the plainer sense. Adam Clarke: Job, having lived soberly and feared God, naturally concluded he would live long and see his posterity multiply as the sands of the seashore. John Wesley draws the sober note, "see how apt even good men are to set death at a distance from them." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the whole confidence touchingly unconscious, the spontaneous hope of a man in prosperity, and records that some would transpose these three verses to the end of the chapter, obviously their natural place in one sense, he grants, though less natural in another, comparing the like displacement at the close of chapter 31. The witnesses do not divide over the pathos: whether Job hoped to multiply his days as the sand or to renew them like the phoenix, the point is the same, a settled expectation of long and peaceful life, uttered by the very man whom the reader knows to be already stripped of nest and brood alike.
19:
Job pictures his old security as a well-watered tree, its "root spread out by the waters" and "the dew" lying "all night upon" its "branch"; and the witnesses debate not the image but the tense in which to read it. The reformed John Gill lays the options out: the words may be taken in the past, as our version has them, giving the grounds of the confidence Job felt in his prosperity; or in the present, "my root is spread out"; or, as some Jewish and Christian interpreters render them, in the future, so that the verse continues Job's hope that things would always stand with him as they then did, and much more abundantly. All three, Gill allows, are true of Job in their way. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott comes down for the present: it is perhaps better to read this verse and the next as "my root is spread out, and the dew lieth; my glory is fresh in me, and my bow is renewed," the language of a man describing a prosperity he still felt unshaken.

On the image itself the witnesses are one. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a metaphor from a healthy tree growing beside a rivulet, which flourishes in all seasons, its leaf never withering nor its fruit falling, and points to the like figure of the blessed man planted by the waters in Ps. 1:3 and Jer. 17:8. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the couplet within their survey of the passage, take the spread root and the night-long dew as the double token of a life fed both from the earth below and the heaven above, moisture at the root and dew on the branch, so that the tree could neither be overturned nor dried up. It is a fruitfulness, they imply, that owes nothing to the tree itself and everything to the waters it was planted by and the dew it lay under, a borrowed flourishing as much as Job's whole estate had been.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense: Job saw himself as a tree so rooted by living water and so bathed in nightly dew that no drought could wither and no storm could fell it. The only real question is whether he speaks of a security remembered, still enjoyed, or expected to endure; and the pathos of the verse, on any tense, is that the reader knows the well-watered tree has since been stripped bare. Job's own confidence, rooted by the waters, is recalled from the far side of the ruin that proved it mortal.
20:
The tree-figure passes into a figure of undimmed vigour, a "glory" still "fresh" in Job and a "bow" "renewed" in his hand; and the witnesses read the two images of freshness and of the bow. The reformed John Gill, in the briefest of notes, keeps alive the tense he had raised in the previous verse: the glory "was," or "is," or "shall be," the same threefold possibility of a thing remembered, present, or expected. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the freshness a vegetative sense, carrying on the tree: Job's glory was fresh as a plant's splendid blossom and large mellow fruit, always in season and in every season; and his bow was renewed, meaning that he was never without the means to accomplish all his wishes, but had prosperity everywhere.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley parts the two clauses cleanly. The "glory" is Job's reputation, which was growing every day; and the "bow" is his strength, so signified because in ancient times the bow and arrows were the principal instruments of war, a usage Wesley grounds in the blessing of Joseph, whose bow abode in strength (Gen. 49:24), and in the song of Hannah, where the bows of the mighty are broken (1 Sam. 2:4). Job's bow renewed in his hand is thus his power, whether to protect himself or to overcome his enemies, ever fresh and never slackened. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the line "mine honour will remain ever fresh to me, and my bow will become young in my hand," catch the same doubleness, an honour that does not fade and a strength that renews its youth.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had gathered the sense of it: God's favour being continued to Job, in the virtue of that his glory was still fresh in him, and it is only by a constant goodness that a man's glory is preserved fresh and kept from withering. So long as that favour lasted, Job found his honour still new and his power still equal to every assault; his bow, renewed in his hand, was the emblem of a strength he thought inexhaustible, so that he feared neither the Sabeans nor the Chaldeans. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse heaps freshness upon freshness, a glory that stayed green, a fame that grew, a bow that kept the suppleness of youth in an aging hand, until the day it was wrested from him and the fresh glory faded in an hour.
21:
The speech circles back from Job's inward vigour to the honour he had abroad, men who "gave ear" and "waited" and "kept silence at my counsel"; and the witnesses hear again the hush of the gate. The reformed John Gill takes the picture as one of universal attention: men gave ear to Job, were all attention and all ear, listening to what he said with the utmost earnestness, high and low, rich and poor, princes and common people alike, and Job concluded, in his confidence, that they always would. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke simply refers the reader back, noting that this is the same idea already drawn in the silence of the princes and the blessing of the ear at vv.9-11, the point resumed to fill out the picture of Job's former sway.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the exact posture the words describe. Men "hearkened to him and waited," and remained silent at his decision, attentive, patient, and ready to be instructed, they listened without interrupting for whatever he should say; and Keil and Delitzsch note the pausal form of the verb "and waited," comparing its like elsewhere, as a small mark of the care with which the poet has drawn the scene. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers it into a single title: Job was the oracle of his country, consulted as an oracle and acquiesced in as one; when others could not be heard, all gave ear to him and kept silence at his counsel, knowing that nothing could be said against it and nothing needed to be added to it. Those that suspected their own judgment, Henry adds, were satisfied in his, and the wrangling parties, when they could agree on nothing else, agreed at least to refer the matter to Job and abide his decision.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse paints the reception every counsellor might envy, a company that gave ear, waited, and fell silent, not out of mere courtesy but out of the certainty that Job's word would settle the matter. It is the same deference the chapter has already shown in the young and the aged, the princes and the nobles, now named directly of Job's "counsel," so that the reader sees the whole assembly bent to catch his judgment. And the tense in which Job recalls it, men "gave ear," is itself the measure of his loss, for the voice they once waited on in silence is now the voice his three friends will scarcely let finish.
22:
The deference deepens into a settled assent: "after my words they spake not again," Job recalls, "and my speech dropped upon them"; and the witnesses take the two clauses as the finality of his word and its gentleness. The reformed John Gill reads the first as unqualified agreement: after Job had spoken, men made no reply, did not attempt to alter his words, add to them, take from them, or contradict them; they "differed not," as one renders it, neither from Job nor among themselves, but rested in what he had said as full to the purpose, after which nothing more could be said. The wesleyan-arminian witnesses dwell on the second clause and its dew. Adam Clarke: Job's speech "dropped upon them," descended as refreshing dew, so that they were encouraged, comforted, and strengthened by it. John Wesley: it dropped "as the rain, which when it comes down gently upon the earth, is most acceptable and beneficial to it."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the couplet and carrying it forward into the verses of the latter rain and the king in the army, take the "dropping" as the distilling of Job's speech upon his hearers, a slow, soaking descent, not a torrent but a nourishing fall. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry joins the two thoughts: after Job's words men spoke not again, for why should any meddle with a subject already exhausted; and his speech dropped upon them as the welcome rain, so that they waited for it as the parched ground waits for showers.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the verse holds two honours together, an authority so complete that none cared to answer, and a manner so gracious that none wished to. Job's word was final without being harsh: it silenced not by overbearing but by satisfying, and it fell on his hearers not as a verdict crushing dissent but as a dew that left them the better for it. The very image of speech that "drops" or "distills" softens the picture of a man before whom the mighty held their peace, for it shows that his power in the gate lay not in the weight of his office but in the refreshment of his wisdom, which men received as the ground receives the rain. It is the counsel of a man loved as much as heeded, whose last word was welcomed rather than merely obeyed.
23:
The dew of the last verse becomes a whole husbandry of longing, men waiting for Job "as for the rain" and opening their mouth wide "as for the latter rain"; and the witnesses explain the two rains of the Eastern year. The reformed John Gill takes the first as the former rain, which fell in autumn after seedtime, about October, to nourish and bring up the seed; as the husbandman waited daily and longingly for it, so the people waited for Job's coming into their assemblies, hungry for his counsel and direction. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the same idea and completes it: they longed to hear Job speak, to receive his counsel and his decisions, as the thirsty land longs for refreshing water; and "they opened their mouth wide" is a metaphor from ground chapped and gaping with long drought. The latter rain, Clarke explains, is that which falls a little before harvest to fill and perfect the grain, as the former rain falls about seedtime to swell the seed and moisten the earth for its nourishment.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the spiritual likeness. The dews of heaven were never so acceptable to the parched ground as Job's wise discourses were to those who attended on them; those are wise, or likely to be, who know how to value wise discourse, who wish for it and wait for it and drink it in as the earth drinks the rain that comes often upon it, after the manner of Heb. 6:7. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, rendering the line among the verses of Job's sovereignty, take the opened mouth as the very gesture of thirst, the hearers gaping for his words as the cracked field gapes for the spring rains that will save the harvest.

The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the double figure measures not Job's authority now but his hearers' appetite, men who did not merely permit his counsel but craved it, waiting on his word as farmers on the rain that stands between them and famine. It is the most flattering of all the images of Job's old honour: not that he was feared, nor even that he was obeyed, but that he was longed for, his speech awaited like the seasonal rains on which a whole year's bread depends. And the ache beneath it is plain, for the man once waited for as the rain now sits on the ash-heap, his counsel unwanted and his comforters turned accusers.
24:
A gentler note closes the picture of Job's sway: "if I laughed on them, they believed it not," and "the light of my countenance they cast not down"; and the witnesses divide over what the disbelief and the undimmed countenance mean. The reformed John Gill takes the laughter as Job's rare condescension to freedom and familiarity: he never laughed in derision, but when in a cheerful mood he would jest with those about him, and they could scarcely believe he was in earnest, so grave and serious a man they knew him to be. Or, Gill adds, following another rendering, "they would not be bold," for Job's familiarity did not breed contempt; they did not presume upon it or grow insolent, but kept their reverence, so that the very point of the words is how great an awe lay upon them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the disbelief rather as the incredulity of joy, comparing the disciples who "believed not for joy" in Luke 24:41: Job's smile was news too good to be true. He would have the words read in the plain indicative, "I laughed on them; they believed it not," and takes the light of Job's countenance as the evidence of his benevolence, which they gave him no occasion to withdraw: they were still worthy of his approbation, and only in the next chapter, Clarke notes, does their change appear. John Wesley joins both halves to the same effect, for Job carried himself so familiarly that they could scarce believe their eyes and ears, and they were cautious to give him no occasion to change his countenance toward them.

So a real, if quiet, difference runs through the verse. Does "they believed it not" mean, with Clarke, Wesley, and Henry, that Job's rare smile was almost too welcome to be credited, or, with Gill's alternative, that his familiarity never tempted them to overstep their reverence? And is it Job who does not cast down the light of his countenance, never changing toward them, or they who took care not to provoke that change? The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott inclines to the first: they would not believe Job could be so affable, could so condescend to them, but looked up to him with the greatest deference. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry holds the affection and the awe together: those on whom Job smiled thought themselves happy and could scarce believe it for joy, yet so wisely did he dispense his favours, and they receive them, that his freedom never made his smiles cheap nor themselves unworthy of the next. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether the wonder be joy or reverence, all agree that Job's kindness was a light his people basked in and were careful never to darken.
25:
The remembrance ends at its height, with Job enthroned among his people, "I chose out their way, and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners"; and the witnesses gather the whole chapter into this last portrait. The reformed John Gill reads the first clause of a trusted counsellor: when his friends and neighbours came to him for advice in civil matters, Job marked out their way, directed what steps to take; and in religious matters he instructed them in their duty toward God and men, proposing what was most eligible in doctrine and practice, for they preferred his judgment to their own and were determined to abide by his choice. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds in the verse Job's whole public and private life at once. As supreme magistrate he chose out their way, adjusted their differences, and sat chief in all their civil assemblies; as a captain-general he dwelt as a king in the midst of his troops, preserving order and discipline; and as a man he did not think himself above the meanest office of kindness, going about comforting the mourners, visiting the sick, and ministering to the afflicted. "Noble Job!" Clarke exclaims, holding him up to the nobles and generals and lords of the earth to imitate his active benevolence.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley parts the titles: men sought Job for advice in all difficult cases, and he directed their methods; he "sat" as a prince or judge while they stood waiting on his counsel; he was "a king" whose presence puts life and courage into a whole army; and he was "as one that comforteth the mourners," whose consolations were always welcome. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry crowns the survey by making Job the sovereign of his country, who chose out their way and steered for them, uniting in himself the authority of a commander who says "Go" and "Come" with the tenderness of a comforter who strengthens the weak hands, a tenderness Job now reflects on with peculiar feeling, being himself a mourner. And Henry, like the older readers, sees in this king who loves righteousness and comforts the perishing a type and figure of Christ, upon whom the blessing of a world ready to perish comes, after the pattern of Ps. 72:2.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott closes on the pathos of the whole backward look. Such is Job's lamentation over the days that were gone; he stands before us as one who has worn the poet's crown of sorrow in remembering happier things in a time of grief, the very type and representative of suffering humanity, of man waiting for redemption but as yet unredeemed, and in that character, Ellicott says, he points us on to Christ, the Redeemer who himself went through all the sorrows of unredeemed men. The witnesses do not divide; they end where Job ends, on the memory of a king among his people, at once ruler, captain, and comforter, whose lost sovereignty becomes, in the reading of the church, a shadow of the King who comforts all that mourn.
